title: Severe bleeding
about: Guides you through first aid in New Zealand when someone is bleeding badly: pressing on the wound, calling 111, a tourniquet on an arm or leg, objects stuck in a wound, a cut-off body part, bleeding inside, and a nosebleed. It keeps the times the ambulance will need.

sources.name: ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.1, First Aid for Management of Bleeding (April 2021, editorial update July 2025) (main source)
Healthify He Puna Waiora, "Bleeding first aid" (reviewed 9 June 2026)

warning: Bleeding badly? Call 111. The sources do not all agree; where they differ, the app shows each one.
audience: Anyone helping a person who is bleeding badly in New Zealand
version: ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.1 'First Aid for Management of Bleeding' (Approved April 2021, supersedes July 2017; Editorial Update July 2025 on tourniquets); Hato Hone St John 'Bleeding' first aid library page (no date shown, footer 2025); Healthify He Puna Waiora 'Bleeding first aid' (Last reviewed 09 Jun 2026); all read 20 Nov 2026

lines.text: Press hard on the wound with a clean cloth, or your hand. Keep the edges of the wound together. Keep pressing.

quotes.text: Firm pressure on or around the wound is the most effective way to stop most bleeding.
If there isn't a cloth nearby, don't waste time – use the person's hand or your hand (wear gloves) to press on the wound and keep the edges of the wound together.

lines.text: Pressure started
Call 111, or get someone else to call. Lie the person down.

quotes.text: Lie the person down, apply pressure and call for an ambulance.
get somebody else to call 111 for you

lines.text: 111 called
Something stuck in the wound? Do not pull it out. Press around it.

quotes.text: Do not remove the embedded object because it may be plugging the wound and restricting bleeding.
use pressure around the object

lines.text: Awake? Check they are happy for you to help. Not awake? Don't delay.

quotes.text: If the person is conscious, check they are happy for you to touch them before you give first aid.
If the person is unconscious and you need to check for injuries or give lifesaving first aid, then don't delay.

lines.text: Gloves (and glasses) if you have them, or a plastic bag over your hands. Don't wait for them.

quotes.text: Use standard precautions (e.g. gloves, protective glasses) if readily available.
If there are no gloves, place your hands inside a plastic bag.

options.label: Other: object stuck, nose, inside, head

lines.text: Keep pressing. Add a second pad and a tighter bandage over the wound.

quotes.text: If bleeding continues, apply a second pad and a tighter bandage over the wound.

lines.text: Second pad added
Still bleeding? Check the pad is right over the bleeding point. If not, take it off and place it again.

quotes.text: check that the pad and bandage are correctly applied, directly over the bleeding.
it may be necessary to remove the pad(s) to ensure that a specific bleeding point has not been missed.

lines.text: Pressing hard on 1 or 2 pads works better than piling on more (ANZCOR).

quotes.text: only using 1 to 2 pads over a small area, will achieve greater pressure over the bleeding point than continuing to layer up further pads.

lines.text: The others differ:
Healthify: add more padding; don't keep lifting it to check.

quotes.text: Keep pressure on and add more padding if needed.
don't keep lifting the dressing to check.

lines.text: St John: keep pressing firmly until the ambulance arrives.

quotes.text: continue to press firmly until the ambulance arrives.

options.label: Yes, from an arm or leg

lines.text: ANZCOR (the joint Australia-NZ guideline) suggests a tourniquet for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that pressure does not stop, if you are trained and have one.

quotes.text: Arterial tourniquets should only be used for life-threatening bleeding from a limb, where the bleeding cannot be controlled by direct pressure.
if trained in its use and one is available.

lines.text: St John and Healthify do not mention tourniquets. They say keep pressing.

quotes.text: Keep pressure on until help arrives or the bleeding stops.

lines.text: ANZCOR treats bleeding as life-threatening if: a limb cut off above the wrist or ankle; a shark attack, propeller cut or similar major injury; pressure does not control it; or signs of shock.

quotes.text: amputated or partially amputated limb above wrist or ankle
shark attack, propeller cuts or similar major trauma to any part of the body
bleeding not controlled by local pressure

options.label: A tourniquet, and I am trained
A tourniquet, but I am not trained

lines.text: ANZCOR suggests a tourniquet "if trained in its use", and says shop-made ones work best when the first aider is trained.

quotes.text: we suggest to apply an arterial tourniquet above the bleeding point, if trained in its use and one is available.
Effective use of commercial tourniquets is optimal when first aid providers are trained in proper application techniques.

lines.text: ANZCOR does not say whether an untrained helper should use one anyway. The app can't decide this for you. The 111 call taker may help.
A shop-made windlass tourniquet works better. In life-threatening bleeding, a home-made one is likely better than none.

quotes.text: Commercially manufactured windlass tourniquets such as those based on military designs are more effective than improvised tourniquets.
in the context of life-threatening bleeding, an improvised tourniquet is likely to be better than no tourniquet.

lines.text: Use a broad band: a triangular or elastic bandage, clothing, or a surfboard leg rope. Tighten it by twisting a rod or stick under the band.

quotes.text: Tourniquets, ideally of a similar broad width to commercial types, can be improvised using materials from a first aid kit (e.g. triangular bandage, elastic bandage) from clothing, a surfboard leg rope or other available similar items.
Improvised tourniquets should be tightened by twisting a rod or stick under the improvised tourniquet band

lines.text: ANZCOR suggests tourniquets "if trained in its use"; it does not say whether that also applies to a home-made one.

quotes.text: if trained in its use and one is available.

lines.text: A thin stretchy blood-test tourniquet will not work. A home-made one that is not tight enough can increase bleeding.

quotes.text: is not suitable for use as an arterial tourniquet.
Improvised tourniquets which do not stop all circulation can increase bleeding.

lines.text: Follow the maker's instructions. No instructions: 5 cm above the bleeding point.

quotes.text: in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions (or 5 cm above the bleeding point if no instructions)

lines.text: If you can, not over a joint, the wound, clothing or a wetsuit. Tighten until the bleeding stops, even if it hurts.

quotes.text: Ideally, a tourniquet should not be applied over a joint or wound
Ideally the tourniquet is not applied over clothing nor wetsuits and is applied tightly, even if this causes local discomfort.
tightened until the bleeding stops.

lines.text: Tap the button the moment it is on. It records the clock time. Tell the paramedics that time.

quotes.text: The time of tourniquet application must be noted and communicated to emergency/paramedic personnel.

lines.text: Tourniquet on
Check where it is and how it is put on. Tighten it.

quotes.text: If a tourniquet does not stop the bleeding its position and application must be checked.

lines.text: Still bleeding? Put on a second tourniquet if you have one, above the first if you can.

quotes.text: a second tourniquet (if available) should be applied to the limb, preferably above the first.

lines.text: Second tourniquet on
Still bleeding after that? ANZCOR: think about a haemostatic dressing as well.

quotes.text: consider using a haemostatic dressing in conjunction with the tourniquet.

options.label: Still bleeding, no dressing: keep pressing

lines.text: Do not take it off. Do not cover it with a bandage or clothing.

quotes.text: the tourniquet should not be removed until the person receives specialist care.
must not be covered up by any bandage or clothing.

lines.text: They need to get to hospital urgently. Tell the paramedics the clock time it went on (on the "Tourniquet on" button and in the Log).

quotes.text: Once applied, the person requires urgent transfer to hospital
The time of tourniquet application must be noted and communicated to emergency/paramedic personnel.

lines.text: No source says how to write the time down (on the tourniquet or the person).
ANZCOR's 2025 update: some studies found possible harm after more than 2 hours, but its advice is unchanged. It gives first aiders no step for this.

quotes.text: this occurred after prolonged (>2 hours) application of arterial tourniquets.
Until the results of this review are available, ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.1 recommendations remain unchanged.

options.label: A cut-off body part to save

lines.text: ANZCOR: no tourniquet, or it did not work? A haemostatic dressing, if you are trained and have one.

quotes.text: from a limb when a tourniquet is not available or has failed to stop the bleeding, we suggest to apply a haemostatic dressing, if trained in its use and one is available.

lines.text: Otherwise keep pressing hard until help arrives. No source gives another step.

quotes.text: Keep pressure on until help arrives or the bleeding stops.

options.label: Still bleeding, no dressing: keep pressing

lines.text: ANZCOR only: a dressing with something in it that helps stop bleeding. Use it if you are trained and have one: where a tourniquet can't go, or when a tourniquet is not there or has not worked.

quotes.text: Haemostatic dressings are impregnated with agents that help stop bleeding.
from a wound site not suitable for tourniquet, or from a limb when a tourniquet is not available or has failed to stop the bleeding

lines.text: Put it as close as you can to the bleeding point. Press it on with your hand, then bandage it in place.

quotes.text: Haemostatic dressings must be applied as close as possible to the bleeding point, held against the wound using local pressure (manually initially) then held in place with the application of a bandage (if available).

lines.text: Haemostatic dressing used
Leave it on until hospital care.

quotes.text: Haemostatic dressings should be left on the bleeding point until definitive care is available.

lines.text: No dressing? Keep pressing hard. No source gives another step.

options.label: Still bleeding, no dressing: keep pressing
Still bleeding from an arm or leg

lines.text: Do not pull it out. It may be plugging the wound.

quotes.text: Do not remove the embedded object because it may be plugging the wound and restricting bleeding.
If an object is stuck in the wound, don't remove it.

lines.text: Put padding around it, on each side. Press on the padding, not on the object.

quotes.text: Apply padding around or on each side of the protruding object, with pressure over the padding.
apply pressure around the wound but don't put pressure on the object.

lines.text: St John differs: remove a small one near the surface (a nail or staple); leave a large one in. The app follows ANZCOR.

quotes.text: If it's small, like a nail or a staple, and near the surface of the skin, remove it.
If it's large, like a screwdriver or a knife, DO NOT remove it.

lines.text: Pressing may not be enough. A tourniquet or haemostatic dressing may still be needed (ANZCOR).

quotes.text: It may still be necessary to use other measures including an arterial tourniquet or haemostatic dressings.

options.label: Still bleeding from an arm or leg
Still bleeding, no dressing: keep pressing

lines.text: Call 111. Press a bulky pad or clean cloth firmly on the bleeding area.

quotes.text: call 111 immediately for an ambulance.
Use a bulky pad or clean cloth and apply it firmly to the bleeding area

lines.text: 111 called
ANZCOR: an arm or leg cut off above the wrist or ankle (even partly) is life-threatening bleeding.

quotes.text: amputated or partially amputated limb above wrist or ankle

lines.text: Raise the injured part? St John and Healthify: yes, if you can. ANZCOR: no evidence it helps; it may cause more pain or injury. The app follows ANZCOR: no raising step.

quotes.text: Keep the injured area raised (if you can).
raise the injured area if possible.
There is no evidence that elevating a bleeding part will help control bleeding and there is the potential to cause more pain or injury.

options.label: Still bleeding from an arm or leg

lines.text: Put the part in a plastic bag; keep it dry. Seal the bag. Put the bag in water with ice.

quotes.text: Put the body part in a sealed plastic bag – keep it dry.
Place the sealed plastic bag in a container of water and ice.

lines.text: Healthify adds: leave a little air in the bag, and use cold water with several ice cubes. ANZCOR says nothing about the part.

quotes.text: seal the bag closed with a little air inside to protect it with a 'cushion' of air.
Place the bag in a bucket of cold water with several ice cubes in the water.

lines.text: Make sure the part goes to hospital with the person.

quotes.text: Make sure the body part goes to the hospital with the person.

steps.title: While you wait for the ambulance

lines.text: Keep pressing until help arrives or the bleeding stops. No source gives a number of minutes.

quotes.text: Keep pressure on until help arrives or the bleeding stops.

lines.text: Keep them lying down, still and warm. Reassure them.

quotes.text: Assist the person into a position of comfort, preferably lying down
Advise the person to lie down and remain still
Keep the person warm
Reassure the person

lines.text: Nothing to eat or drink, not even medicines.

quotes.text: Do not give any food or drink orally, including medications

lines.text: Check their breathing and how they are often. ANZCOR gives no time.

quotes.text: Monitor the vital signs at frequent intervals

lines.text: Arm or leg: ANZCOR says keep it still. Raise it? St John says yes; ANZCOR says there is no evidence it helps and it may cause more pain or injury. The app follows ANZCOR.

quotes.text: Restrict movement by immobilising a bleeding limb
If the wound is on the person's arm or leg, raise it up (to reduce blood flow to the injured area).
There is no evidence that elevating a bleeding part will help control bleeding and there is the potential to cause more pain or injury.

options.label: A cut-off body part to save

lines.text: ANZCOR: pale and sweaty with a pulse over 100, or capillary refill over 2 seconds, and/or less awake.

quotes.text: pale and sweaty plus pulse rate >100, or capillary refill > 2 sec and/or decreased level of consciousness

lines.text: Healthify: pale, clammy, sweaty, fast breathing, confused, fainting, or not conscious.

quotes.text: unusual paleness or loss of colour, clammy skin, sweating, fast breathing, confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness.

lines.text: Call 111 if nobody has. Keep them lying down and warm. Nothing to eat or drink.

quotes.text: the person shows signs of shock.
Help the person lie down if possible and keep them warm.

lines.text: 111 called
ANZCOR says "treat shock" but gives no steps here. Check them often (no time given). Oxygen only if you have it and are trained.

quotes.text: Treat shock
Monitor the vital signs at frequent intervals
Administer oxygen if available and trained to do so

lines.text: Bleeding badly? Stopping the bleeding comes first, before airway and breathing (ANZCOR).

quotes.text: In life-threatening bleeding, control of bleeding takes priority over airway and breathing interventions.

lines.text: Call 111 if nobody has. Not responding and not breathing normally: start CPR (Healthify); follow the Basic Life Support flowchart (ANZCOR).

quotes.text: If the person isn't responding and isn't breathing normally, start CPR.
If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow the Basic Life Support Flowchart.

lines.text: 111 called
Bleeding that is not life-threatening: airway and CPR come first (ANZCOR).

quotes.text: where control of bleeding follows establishing airway and commencing CPR if required.

lines.text: No source says what one helper alone should do when both are needed. These sources give no CPR steps. Follow the 111 call taker.

options.label: Bruise or swelling on an arm or leg

lines.text: Think of it if there are signs of shock, pain or swelling, or blood coughed up, vomited, or in pee or poo (or black, tar-like poo).

quotes.text: should always be suspected where there are symptoms and signs of shock.
have pain, tenderness or swelling over the affected area
cough up blood or have blood in their vomit, urine or poo, or have black tar-like poo

lines.text: ANZCOR adds: bleeding from the vagina or penis, and severe bleeding in pregnancy.

quotes.text: vaginal bleeding or bleeding from the penis
Severe bleeding may also occur from complications of pregnancy.

lines.text: Call 111. Help them lie down; keep them warm. Loosen tight clothes. Nothing to eat or drink.

quotes.text: Send for an ambulance.
Help the person lie down and keep them warm.
Loosen any tight clothes, especially around their neck or waist.
Do not let the person eat or drink anything.

lines.text: 111 called
Raise the legs? Healthify: slightly, unless it hurts or a leg may be injured. ANZCOR and St John do not say.

quotes.text: If possible, raise their legs slightly unless this causes pain or you suspect a leg injury.

lines.text: Put them on their side. Stay with them until help arrives.

quotes.text: If they become unconscious, put them on their side if they're breathing.
Stay with them and reassure them until help arrives.

steps.title: Bruise on an arm or leg

lines.text: No bleeding outside: press on it, with a cold pack if you have one.

quotes.text: If there is bruising to a limb and no external bleeding, we suggest to use pressure and a cold pack if available.

lines.text: Call 111 if it is badly swollen or painful, or they show signs of shock.

quotes.text: If closed bleeding in a limb is causing severe swelling or pain, or the person is showing signs of shock

lines.text: 111 called
Press firmly on the wound to slow the bleeding.

quotes.text: If the person is bleeding from a head injury, apply direct firm pressure to the wound to stem the bleeding.

lines.text: Skull may be broken? Healthify says do not press.

quotes.text: But don't apply pressure if you think they might have a skull fracture.

lines.text: Only Healthify covers head wounds, under its minor bleeding heading.
Healthify: do not press on it.

quotes.text: But don't apply pressure if you think they might have a skull fracture.

lines.text: Call 111.

quotes.text: If you have a person in urgent need of medical attention, call 111 now.

lines.text: 111 called
No source says how to slow the bleeding instead. Follow the 111 call taker.
Call 111. If you can, move the heavy weight off them.

quotes.text: If possible, move the heavy weight off the person.

lines.text: 111 called
Press a clean cloth or pad firmly on any bleeding. Support the injured part with blankets or clothes.

quotes.text: Stop any bleeding by pressing a clean cloth or pad firmly on the area.
support the injured area with blankets or clothes.

lines.text: Watch them closely for any change.

quotes.text: Watch the person closely for any change in their condition.

lines.text: Only St John covers crush injuries.
Sit them down, leaning forward. Pinch the soft part of the nose, both sides, below the bony bridge.

quotes.text: The person should sit down and lean forward.
Pressure must be applied equally to both sides of the nose, over the soft part below the bony bridge

lines.text: Breathe through the mouth. Spit out blood; don't swallow it.

quotes.text: breathe through their mouth while pinching their nose (the soft part)
Encourage the person to spit out blood rather than swallow it

lines.text: Pinching started
After a head injury (such as a broken skull)? Call 111 (St John).

quotes.text: If bleeding from the nose is due to a head injury e.g., a fractured skull

options.label: A child: something stuck in the nose

quotes.text: The person should remain seated at total rest for at least 10 minutes.

reminders.text: Nosebleed 20 minutes: still bleeding? Get help

quotes.text: If bleeding continues for more than 20 minutes seek medical assistance.

lines.text: Keep pinching and resting, seated. How long differs:
ANZCOR: at least 10 minutes.

quotes.text: The person should remain seated at total rest for at least 10 minutes.

lines.text: ANZCOR: at least 20 minutes on a hot day or after exercise.

quotes.text: On a hot day or after exercise, it might be necessary to maintain pressure for at least 20 minutes.

lines.text: St John: pinch for 10 to 20 minutes.

quotes.text: for 10 to 20 minutes.

lines.text: The 20-minute bar counts from opening the nosebleed screen.

options.label: A child: something in the nose

lines.text: Still bleeding after 20 minutes, or after a head injury: St John says call 111. ANZCOR says get medical help after 20 minutes.

quotes.text: if it doesn't stop after 20 minutes then call 111 for an ambulance
If bleeding continues for more than 20 minutes seek medical assistance.

lines.text: 111 called
Keep pinching and leaning forward while you wait.

quotes.text: The person should lean with the head forward to avoid blood flowing down the throat.

lines.text: Tell the helpers when pinching started (on its button and in the Log).
Something stuck in a child's nose (like a bead or coin)? Do not remove it. It may cause more damage.

quotes.text: If the person is a child, check if anything is stuck in their nose e.g., a bead or coin.
If there is, DO NOT remove it (that may cause further damage).

lines.text: St John gives no next step. In urgent need of medical help, call 111 now.

quotes.text: If you have a person in urgent need of medical attention, call 111 now.

lines.text: 111 called
Do not blow the nose for a few hours.

quotes.text: When the bleeding has stopped the person should not blow their nose for a few hours.

lines.text: Tourniquet on? Tell them the clock time it went on. The "Tourniquet on" button recorded it; it is also in the Log.

quotes.text: The time of tourniquet application must be noted and communicated to emergency/paramedic personnel.

lines.text: The Log also has when 111 was called, pressure started, and any second pad, second tourniquet or haemostatic dressing.
A cut-off body part goes to hospital with them: in a sealed bag, kept dry, in water with ice.

quotes.text: Make sure the body part goes to the hospital with the person.
Put the body part in a sealed plastic bag – keep it dry.
Place the sealed plastic bag in a container of water and ice.

lines.text: Only the tourniquet time is asked for by a source; the rest of this list is the app's.
